On the orders of the day:

I would draw the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals to an interview given at Montreal by Mr. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. May I be permitted to preface a question I am going to ask by stating that the interview is based upon a report submitted to the house in reply to a question asked by me some time ago concerning the amount of subsidies in land and cash given to the Canadian Pacific and its subsidiaries by the federal government? In this interview Mr. Beatty denies the accuracy of the statement submitted to the house by the Canadian National Railways through the Department of Railways and Canals. speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
Yesterday evening the hon, member for Gloucester drew to my attention the interview of Mr. Beatty and therefore I made some inquiries regarding it. The hon. member submitted to the house five different series of questions, and I think each series contained five or more questions, so that there were altogether some twenty-five or more. Those questions related to specific subjects. As the hon. gentleman has pointed out, one of the series referred to land grants and cash aid to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and matters of that sort. The questions asked did not refer to other matters to which Mr. Beatty referred in the statement made to the press. The information which we obtained, which was partly supplied through the Department of the Interior, as to land grants for example, was from recognized sources and is in accordance with the statistics as given out by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics for many years. For example in regard to the 26,000,000 acres of land to which Mr. Beatty refers, on page 12 of the Statistics of Steam Railways in Canada for the year ended December 31, 1933, exactly the same figures are given as those which we gave to the hon. gentleman, or which were given by the Department of the Interior in the returns furnished. Naturally we did not deal with the entire question of money grants or other grants to the Canadian National for instance, to some of which Mr. Beatty referred. But this blue book as put out for many years gives exactly the same figures as those in the return furnished to the hon. gentleman. There is nothing new in the figures, they are the same as submitted to the royal commis-

sion on railways. I do not wish to deal with the question further than that except to say that the figures given have been of public record for many years, and no exception has been taken to them as far as the land grants or other figures submitted are concerned.

speechtext:
With regard to
subsection 4 of clause 20, I have had the question carefully looked into, and I have decided in my own mind at all events that this clause is quite in order as it is printed. Its purpose is to provide that any three days of unemployment, whether consecutive or not in any week, will be counted as continuous unemployment in order to qualify a man for the benefit of this legislation. The man is unemployed this week for three days; next week he is unemployed for another three days, making six days of continuous unemployment. If he is unemployed for three days the following week that makes nine days of continuous unemployment. There is no restriction in this section of the bill to any particular week. Yesterday the hon. member for Comox-AIberni (Mr. Neill) argued that this section applied only to the first two weeks. I do not read it that way at all. It states:
-any two such continuous periods-
That does not refer only to the first one and two; it refers equally to the second and third or the third and fourth. That is the way 1 read the act, and that is the way it is interpreted by the officer of the Justice department with whom I discussed it this morning. Further I take it the bon. member for Comox-AIberni argued that because nine days of unemployment is required to qualify in this country while only six days is required in Great
Unemployment Insurance

Britain, this section should read a little differently. As a matter of fact a man can come under this section, in my judgment and in the judgment of the officer of the department whom I consulted, after having three days of unemployment in each of three consecutive weeks, making nine days in all, or in the weeks that come afterward providing there are at least two such periods in each six weeks. This section is based on the British act. I would refer the hon. gentleman to page 34 of the evidence taken before the royal commission in Great Britain, where he will find the British interpretation of this section, which amply supports this view.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: Do I understand that if a man coming under this act is unemployed for three days in each of three weeks then he becomes entitled to unemployment benefits in the event of three ensuing then three more days of employment before the next three days of unemployment, or if any period of employment ensues? subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION

Determination of Questions
27. (1) If any question arises-
(a)	as to whether any employment or any class of employment is or will be such employment as to make the person engaged therein an employed person within the meaning of this act or whether a person is or was an employed person within the meaning of this act; or
(b)	whether a person or class of persons is or is not, or was or was not, a person or class of persons to whom a special or supplementary scheme under this act applies or applied; or
(c)	as to who is or was the employer of any employed person; or
(d)	as to the rate of contribution payable under or in pursuance of this act by or in respect of any person or class of persons or as to the rates of contribution payable in respect of any employed person by the employer and that person respectively; or
(e)	whether a person was or was not employed in any excepted employment during any period falling within the period of two years specified in the first statutory condition; the question shall be decided by the commission: Provided that the commission may. if they think fit, instead of themselves deciding such question, refer the question for decision to the exchequer court.
(2)	In determining any question as to whether any occupation, in which a person is or has been engaged, is or was such as to make him an employed person within the meaning of this act, regard shall be had to the nature of the work on which he is or was engaged rather than to the business of the person by whom he is or was employed.
(3)	The commission may, on new facts being brought to their notice, revise any decision given under this section.
(4)	The governor in council may make regulations prescribing the procedure under this section.
I believe that complies with the understanding at which we arrived yesterday. Therefore I move, seconded by Mr. Murphy that the section I have read be substituted for section 27 as printed.

speechtext: This subsection was discussed at great length yesterday and this morning I have had the opportunity to give it some further consideration. My view is that it is the duty of the worker to see that the stamps are put in his book. We do not wish to accept the suggestion made by hon. members to the effect that the state should lose the money in the event of an employer accepting the workman's share and not turning it in to the fund. All these contributions are paid by way of revenue stamps. It is necessary that the workmen should do their share towards seeing that these stamps are put in their books at the proper time. If they do that there can- be no chance of loss to the workers.

and the employer fails to pay to the fund, the workman will have the right of civil action against the employer.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I believe that would not be so in practical operation. In a big steel company, for example, where there are 4,000 or 5,000 employees I believe we will find that the books containing the stamps will be kept by the employer during the time the man works for him.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: What about the smaller fellow?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION

speechtext: Yes, that is true; they would go only once. In big firms that is the way it would be done, and I believe the acting Prime Minister will find that is the way it is done in England, too.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I believe the evidence given before the price spreads committee shows that on many occasions the minimum wage legislation has not been lived up to, and that the employee has not been in a position to enforce it. The employer would simply refuse to give the minimum wage, and there have been all sorts of tricks used to get over the difficulty. In those cases the employee has had to coniform to the wishes of the employer, or lose his job. I believe it is unfair to place the onus upon the employee.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
It is sometimes said that we are very far removed from the common people. I do not believe that fact could be better illustrated than by the argument now raised by the acting Prime Minister. Picture to yourselves men out in the bush, connected with logging camps, coming in to the office and demanding to see their books to find out if the stamps have been put in. Picture them arguing with the boss and quoting section 33 of the act indicating that they are liable to a loss which they do not purpose suffering. A working man, a logger, is supposed to be familiar with a very complicated section of this act, and we are supposing that he will come into the office and demand his rights. If we could grasp the point of view as to what would happen to that man I believe we would make a change in this section. He is to have the whole responsibility of enforcing a law which has been forced
upon him-there is compulsory contribution -and he must line up the boss and say to that gentleman, "I do not believe you put those stamps on my book last week; I want proof." The boss would say, "What! Don't you think my word is good? You ought to be a lawyer. We can get along without you; you know too much about the act. We can get along without your services." In the environment of this chamber it sounds all right to say that it is the duty of the man to see that the stamps are put on, but in actual practice it will be impossible for him to do so-at any rate, if not impossible it will be impracticable. And if he tried to do it he would be a marked man.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext: I am sorry that the right hon. gentleman who has charge of this bill has not seen fit to make the alterations suggested yesterday in connection with this clause. The general fund out of which the insurance will be ultimately paid is of course provided by the state, the employer and the employee, and it is supposed to be an insurance fund. In the clause before us it is assumed that the workman has paid his share, but that the employer has failed to pay into the fund, in which case the employee is deprived of his insurance, and the only thing that is given to him in return is his right to sue his employer in the courts for neglect of duty. I want to emphasize the point made so strongly yesterday by the hon. member for Bow River and others, that the employee should not be penalized in any way for the default of his employer. If he has paid in his share he should have the right to draw from the fund. If there is any individual who has violated the provisions of the act that individual should be prosecuted by the government itself and it should not be left to the employee to take action.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
The Workmen's Compensation Act is a practical example of the point under consideration. A good many problems would arise under that act if the responsibility were left to the employee to see that the employer discharged his obligation. That responsibility rests with the board, and I think it will be found when this act gets into practical application that the money for the stamps will be deducted from the pay envelope of the employee. That is the way it is done in Great Britain, and a regulation to that effect will be necessary. If you leave it to all these fellows to chase around getting stamps, a good many of them will not get the stamps.

Unemployment Insurance

I have had experience with union dues and I know that all the king's horses and all the king's men will not make them do it. It is absolutely unfair to place the responsibility on the employee of prosecuting the employer if he has not complied with the law. I could understand it if the scheme were voluntary; but where you have a compulsory insurance scheme I think the obligation rests squarely on the shoulders of the government.

The Workmen's Compensation Act as it operates in British Columbia affords a good example. There the procedure is to collect a percentage of the pay roll, and an inspector comes along once or twice a year and checks up the books of the company. He says, "There is so much due from the company." I have known of cases where companies were hundreds and thousands of dollars in arrears. The government gets after them, pointing out that the money should have been paid at the stated time. But it was not paid, and when the slump came it was discovered that the fund created by these payments had been enormously overdrawn because these people had not observed their obligations. In some instances they have gone bankrupt and owed the government thousands of dollars. If we had the sample section as in this bill, some man looking for compensation would be told,

"I am sorry you cannot get compensation because the money was not paid over, although perhaps eventually you may collect it from the employer." The Prime Minister did not agree with me the other day when I gave a parallel instance. If I pay my taxes and the government agent to whom I hand over the money absconds with it, all that is required of me is to produce evidence that I paid it to the official authorized to receive it. The government does not come along and say that because the man to whom I paid the money absconded I shall have to pay it again. The absurdity there is apparent, and the case here is similar, only it is worse, because the man in this instance has not an opportunity to see that the money is sent in. If the workmen went into the office to see about the stamps at the end of each week, and if five or six hundred people came into the office demanding to see the actual stamps placed in the book, they would be called bolsheviks or reds. Following up the argument

If the risk is to be borne individually, as it appears to be proposed under this bill, there is no longer any insurance, so that that most important element of this whole bill disappears; if there is no insurance, it is no longer an unemployment insurance bill. Insurance in any phase of it implies a number of people dividing up the risk, and when one fails to meet that risk, then the others are called upon to meet it. In this case, all those others are represented by the commission. The commission collects from everyone in order to be able to distribute the benefits, and if I understand this article correctly, the benefits will not bn distributed to the insured unless each individual company is in a position to make the payments required under the bill. That destroys every vestige of an insurance principle as contained in this measure. The point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is in my opinion well taken, and the government should clearly state in the bill that the commission should be responsible for the payment of the benefits. The government may make any other provision it wishes as to how the contributions are to be collected; that is not of great importance, but the important point is that the commission should be responsible for the payment of the benefits which are conferred upon the individual workman by the bill.

speechtext:
Yes; I have the statement here, with regard to excepted occupations. This is a memorandum prepared by Mr. A. D. Watson, chief actuary of the department of Insurance, and Mr. M. C. Maclean, of the bureau of statistics:
Excepted Employments
Stated in general terms, unemployment insurance can only be satisfactorily extended

Unemployment Insurance
to persons in employments where there is a material degree of unemployment and where the employment is carried on at such places and under such conditions that is it reasonably practicable to adapt a scheme of unemployment insurance with real advantage to the persons insured.
It is rather difficult to know in advance of actual contact with the problems of unemployment in many occupations, especially in a country such as Canada, just how far it may be practicable to go on the start. It is best, however, that the initial difficulties of getting a scheme set up should not be accentuated by bringing in employments which will result in very special problems before the machinery and technique of administration are sufficiently devoloped. A glance at the employments covered by the British scheme of 1911 makes it possible to get a concrete notion of the characteristics of any employment which is fairly easily insurable.
The British scheme of 1911 applied to all manual workers over 16 years of age in the following trades; mechanical engineering, ironfounding, shipbuilding, construction of vehicles, sawmilling and machine woodwork when carried on in connection with an insured trade or of a kind commonly conducted in connection with such a trade, and construction of such works as railroads, docks. harbours, etc. The workers insured numbered about 2,500,000 in the whole of the United Kingdom.
It will be noted that in all employments of the above classes there would generally be

(i)	a more or less fixed place of employment;
(ii)	no persons in the occupation working on their own account or on shares;
(iii)	a substantial number of workers to one employer;
(iv)	a concentration of workers and that not usually in remote places; and
(v)	no very marked seasonal fluctuations in work.
Having regard for the administrative machinery of the bill, it will be seen how important these characteristics of employments are. The whole administration centres about the employment office or branch. It is at the employment office that an insured person gets his unemployment book when entering insurable employment and he returns his unemployment book there as soon as he is out of work. While unemployed he will in general be required to register from time to time at the employment office; it is there he will look for information concerning work; and it is there that he will receive the payments of his insurance benefit. There is necessarily a limit to the number of employment offices and branches which can be established, and to be of service insured persons must be relatively near an office.
Furthermore, a measure such as we have in this bill must be enforced both with respect to employers of labour and with respect to employees. There must be no evasion of the requirements of the scheme by either employers or employees. To this end an elaborate inspec-tional service will be necessary. Inspectors must know where employment is supposed to be carried on, and if the area covered should be too great relatively to the number employed the cost would be prohibitive. In this connection reference may be made to section 34 to get a picture of what will be necessary by way of inspection to see that the act is being properly complied with, and with that picture in mind an examination of excepted employments very generally will show the difficulties of administration which would be encountered from this point of view alone.
Again, some occupations are so highly seasonal, especially in some parts of the country, that if workers therein were insured they would have little or no opportunity to qualify for insurance and obtain unemployment benefit within the normal season.
It was not until 1916 that any enlargement of insurable employment was made in Britain. In that year munition workers and allied trades which would be adversely affected by the termination of the war were brought under the scheme. But it was not until 1920 that the application of the scheme was made fairly general to all wage-earners except persons employed in agriculture, horticulture, forestry, private domestic service and numerous specified employments some of them of a miscellaneous character.
Thus it was only after nine years of experience that the scheme was made about as comprehensive in its scope as the scheme of the bill before the house. By availing ourselves of the experience gained in Britain over the past twenty-four years, it is believed that in Canada it is not a greater experiment than undertaken in Britain in 1911 to start with a scheme about as extensive in its scope as now in operation over there. Likewise, it is believed that it would not be wise to attempt at the beginning to out-run British experience.
In particular, it may be noted that agriculture, including horticulture and forestry, are not yet included in the scheme in Britain. In January of this year the unemployment insurance statutory committee made a report on a scheme of insurance for agriculture. It is clear from that report that new and serious difficulties will be confronted in the administration of such a scheme as recommended. The conditions of wage earners in agriculture in Canada differ so fundamentally from conditions in England that there is no prospect that a similar scheme would be appropriate here. Conditions vary widely in agriculture in different parts of Canada and employment is far more seasonal in some parts than in others. It is in fact only after a most careful survey of the whole Canadian field that a scheme can be devised to meet the needs of agricultural workers. For this provision has been made in section 7 of the bill.
Having dealt at some length with the underlying conditions which make unemployment insurance a_ practical proposition, and with the difficulties inherent in insuring agriculture, it will perhaps be clear enough the insurance of employment in fishing and logging will require careful and mature consideration. It would be a disservice to persons working in these occupations to bring them under a scheme of insurance almost certainly unsuited to their needs. The seasonal difficulties, especially in certain parts of the country, are most serious.
The insurance of stevedores has given rise to more intractable problems in England' than any other class of insured employment. It is intended that the needs of these workers
Unemployment Insurance

should also be carefully studied before they are either brought under the general scheme or a special scheme. It should be clear that any scheme applied to them or to any other class of workers will on the whole be for their advantage before being made effective.
Coming now to employment in banking and insurance, which employments are also excluded, it is to be noted that even through this long depression banks and insurance companies have not found reductions in staff necessary. By refraining from making new appointments, the natural decreases in staff through retirements, death, marriage of females, and so on, it has generally not been found necessary to decrease staff on account of reduction of work arising out of the depression. It would therefore appear that insurance for such employment would be somewhat analogous to insurance for a fireproof building; the contributions would be required without any material benefit in return.
If in the light of what has been already said, the other excepted employments are considered with care, it will be found that they have been excluded on sound grounds.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me this is a most unsatisfactory statement. It may be all very well from a purely actuarial standpoint, and it may be satisfactory from the point of view that the government does not desire to involve itself in any obligations. It is highly unsatisfactory however from the standpoint of providing for the needs of the unemployed workers. I believe it is fair and reasonable at this point to recall the circumstances under which the unemployment insurance legislation was brought down. We were practically informed that the government was about to bring in a splendid scheme which to a large extent would solve the problem of unemployment among the workers. I am sure it was a shock to the entire country when the Prime Minister upon introducing this legislation stated it would not touch the needs of any men or women now unemployed.
For me it is an equally great shock to find a large number of excepted classes, thereby rendering the legislation of very little service to those who most need it.

Unemployment Insurance

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH AN UNEMPLOYMENT AND SOCIAL INSURANCE COMMISSION
speechtext:
Yes; of course, we have introduced legal matters, and so on, to bring it up to date, but with regard to the point under discussion we are back where Great Britain was twenty-five years ago. We are accepting what to them was tentative legislation. In 1916 Great Britain, faced with a serious unemployment crisis, broadened her legislation. Again, in 1920, nearly all the workers with the exception of those engaged in agriculture were brought within the scope of the legislation. Now they are bringing in even those agricultural workers. That is the development which has taken place in Great Britain in the last twenty-five years. But in this country we seem to be satisfied with the first faltering steps Great Britain took. We disregard the experience she has had in these past twenty-five years. While as regards social legislation we may be twenty-five years behind Great Britain, I do not think we are twenty-five years behind her so far as social conditions are concerned. We have just as much need for advanced legislation as has Great Britain.
I would point out, further, that the memorandum read by the acting Prime Minister calls special attention to the differences between conditions in Canada and those in Great Britain. We have greater irregularity in our labour; we have certain seasonal fluctuations; our workers live long distances from public offices. I recognize that these are difficulties. Of course, it would be a great deal easier if we lived in a small compact island. It would be a great deal easier if the greater part of our population were engaged in industrial work. It would be a great deal easier if we had a more equable climate. It would be a great deal easier if we had not the divisions of the nine provinces. It would be a great deal easier if our workers lived in the cities instead of on the far flung frontiers. But then we are not dealing with a situation of that sort; we are dealing with Canada as it is, a Canada in w'hich a great part of the population is still engaged in agriculture and the other primary industries and is likely to be so engaged for a good many years to come. We are dealing with a country that extends between three and four thousand miles; a country in which there are these various provincial difficulties; a country in which the workers are scattered in construction camps, logging camps, mining camps, in the most remote districts. I submit therefore that this legislation should not be brought down to suit conditions as they existed in England twenty-five years ago but to suit conditions in Canada in this year, 1935; and any legislation that does not do that is hardly worth the paper it is written on.
I do not want to go into all the details of these excepted employments, but I would urge the necessity for dealing with those engaged in agricultural work. We have had in the past a very large army who were engaged part of the time in our cities and part of the time in rural work. In fact, I do not know how we could have managed in the past to harvest our crops in the west unless we had had the assistance of large numbers who were for part of the time engaged in logging or construction work or farm work in other areas. Hon. members will recall the excursions we used to have from east to west, but as a result of combines and other machinery, that has not been quite so necessary in recent years. But we still have large numbers who are engaged for part of the time in other work and part of the time in agriculture, and any scheme of unemployment insurance which is to be at all adequate should look after this class of people, and should seek to dovetail one occupation into the other. I do urge that we shall not begin to solve the problem which ought to come within the scope of an unemployment insurance scheme until we look after these people who at least part of the time are engaged in agricultural or horticultural or forestry operation.
I come now to fishing. Admittedly the situation differs widely on the west coast from the situation which we find in the east or in some of the lake districts in the central part of the country. Here again there is great necessity for some provision to be made during off season for those engaged in fishing. It is not always the same kind of fishing; one group of men are engaged in one type of fishing at one season and in another type of fishing in another season. And some are engaged in fishing for part of the year and during another part of the year in the tillage of their own soil. Surely this class of people should be cared for. We have already had a slight enlargement of the scope of the act with regard to lumbering and logging. I do not think I need remind the committee that the conditions vary very greatly in British Columbia from those that prevail in the northern sections of the central provinces and again from those in the mari-times. But logging is one of the primary industries of the country; in the past it has been one of the outlets for the unemployed during a part of the year. It seems to me that anything like a proper scheme of unemployment insurance, adequate to meet the needs of the country, ought to look after all those engaged in that great primary industry.
I will not discuss in detail the occupations of hunting and trapping. These may present a greater difficulty because of the character of
Unemployment Insurance

the occupation; but certainly hunting and trapping-and I would include prospecting- ought to come within the purview of 'the unemployment insurance commission. Then there is transportation. We have very large numbers of people engaged in transportation by water in our ports both east and west. Above the main door of this building we find this reference to the sea:
The wholesome sea is at her gates Her gates both east and west.
But so far as this legislation is concerned we are excluding the people that go down to the sea in ships; we are excluding them almost entirely from the scope of our legislation. I would like to refer particularly to stevedoring. Undoubtedly there was a great deal of difficulty with this class of work in England, but they did manage to a large extent to regularize it. It is different with us, because all our ports are not deep water ports. In Montreal the workers are engaged in stevedoring for part of the year and during the other part of the year they find other occupations. A commission charged with the functions which this commission will perform ought to take into their cognizance the whole of the stevedoring business and seek to dovetail one occupation into another. Otherwise what will these people do? Are they to be on public charity for a part of the year-and this through no fault of their own? I think it is absurd. In the deep water ports, where the regular steamers ply, we might succeed largely in regularizing the stevedoring occupation. As it is to-day, however, it is casual work that attracts the unemployed from other parts of the country, and unless the situation is dealt with there will be trouble in the days to come.
I am not at all convinced by what * the memorandum states with regard to those engaged in the banking, mortgage, loan, trust, insurance and other financial businesses. What does this memorandum say? It says that owing to the peculiar conditions of the last few years a great many of these people have had to be turned off and that we have pretty nearly reached rock botton, or something of that kind. But that is no reason why those engaged in these occupations today should not be looked after. We were told in the earlier part of the memorandum that the underlying principle was that there must be some material degree of employment, regularity of employment. Surely bank clerks and those engaged in insurance companies ought to come under that head. I cannot see, according to the very principles enunciated in the memorandum itself, why these should not be included. Then we come to
[Mr I. A. Mackenzie.]
unemployment in domestic service, where the unemployed person was employed in clubs or in any business carried on for purposes of gain. Again, the same thing applies. Why should people in domestic service not have some protection? I ask the acting Prime Minister why he has not followed the British lead in this regard, whether he would take the trouble before this is passed to study the British act and find out what are its provisions, according to its latest amendment, and adopt these provisions in that regard just as much as in regard to the other clause we were discussing a few minutes ago. The same with respect to professional nurses and probationers training in the hospitals, and teachers of all kinds. Why should not these come under an unemployment insurance scheme? A great many of them have no unemployment insurance schemes of their own. And why not include many of our civil servants who do not come under the superannuation act and hence cannot get any benefit therefrom? Why should not these classes in our community come under the scheme? I can understand that if the scheme is to be on a purely actuarial basis there may have to be a gradation in payments. In fact, I am not at all sure that a flat rate is a fair way of collecting, because there are some who are receiving a comparatively high income and some a very low income. Why should they all have to pay a flat rate? I cannot see the justice of that. If it is to be a pure insurance scheme, the benefits ought to be in proportion to the amounts paid in. We were told yesterday that we ought to be willing to be our brother's keeper. If we are to go on the principle not of an absolutely sound insurance scheme but rather on the more general altruistic basis of the strong sharing the burdens of the weak, why do we not include in this scheme the poorly paid classes in the community or those who are more frequently out of work? In this connection I might as well read to the committee a statement which I promised to submit-a statement received a few days ago from the executive board of the All Canadian Congress of Labour. They are urging that the bill be amended in two important respects:
First, it is submitted that the rate of contributions provided in the bill as introduced is beyond the means of workers receiving low wages and that the graduation according to age and sex should be replaced by a scale of contributions according to earnings.
Comparison may be made between the case of a woman earning, say, $125 a month in a railway office and that of a railwayman, who, through demotion due to staff reduction, is earning only $45 a month in full-time employ-

Unemployment Insurance
ment. It is felt that the requirement to pay a dollar or more per month out of wages which may be as low as from $45 to $75 a month will inflict a real hardship on many workers; it is certain that it will place beyond their reach the protection which they might secure by membership in a labour union, by rendering it impossible for them to pay union, dues.
Second, it is submitted that the qualifying period for benefit under the unemployment insurance provisions of the bill should be reduced from forty to twenty-six weeks, at least at the inception of the scheme, in order to make the benefits available without unreasonable delay. Should this change disturb the actuarial basis of the scheme it is felt that the present stressful conditions would warrant temporarily a larger measure of assistance for the fund from the public treasury, it being recognized that such additional assistance would be largely compensated bv the reduction in the cost of relieving destitution.
It is not my purpose at this point unduly to labour these arguments, but I wish to put before the committee the seriousness of limiting the scheme as the government has done. Had the expectation of the workers not been so buoyed up, the situation would not perhaps have been so bad. When I was a boy, we used to keep hens and when we heard a great cackling in the henyard, we went out feeling quite sure there was an egg laid. In this case there was a tremendous cackling long before the egg was laid. Now when we come to look for the egg, it is such a tiny peewee of an egg, we hardly know whether it is worth anything or not. In all seriousness, I presume the government is in earnest in bringing down a bill which will help the situation in Canada, but if in our act we adopt a twenty-five year old model, that does not begin to touch the situation which actually faces us. I repeat we ought to face not the situation which they faced in England long before the war, but that which faces us to-day in the post-war period. We should recognize the very serious depression with which we are and may be confronted for a good many years to come.
Sir GEORGE PERLEY; I am not claiming that this bill embraces as much as does the present British act, but the hon. gentleman is entirely wrong in claiming that this bill goes no further than the original British act that was passed as far back as 1911. A memorandum I have states that it was only after nine years of experience that the British scheme was made about as comprehensive in its scope as is the bill at present before our house. In other words they started quietly and by experience they learned and made changes in their act. That is what we are doing to-day. This bill is brought in for the purpose of covering as many of the people
of this country as possible, but it is not final; it is not supposed to be a measure that will not be amended to advantage by succeeding parliaments. I hope it will be so amended; we want to make it as effective as possible, and if the hon. gentleman thinks no egg was laid, he ought to get his glasses enlarged so that he may have a better chance of understanding the matter. He has overlooked also the clause in the bill giving authority to the commission to consider matters of this kind, that is the question of excepted employees. Clause 7 reads;
In addition to the powers and duties of the commission as otherwise provided by this act, the commission shall, as soon as practicable after appointment, undertake investigations for the purpose of making proposals to the governor in council for-
(a) providing unemployment insurance for the employments excepted from the operation of part III of this act, or for any of them, either by extending thereto the provisions of that part, with such modifications, if any, as may be found necessary, or by special or supplementary schemes.
In other words, it is definitely contemplated in this bill that it is not a final measure and that the commission shall look into any questions which may be raised regarding excepted types of workers and make recommendations to the governor in council, so that when parliament meets again, this bill may be amended if it is found advisable to do so, or if there is any way in which it can be improved. The hon. gentleman, very wisely, voted for the second reading of this bill which is a good one. It may not go so far as he would like, but at all events it is the beginning of a first class piece of legislation which is for the good of the country. I think he makes a mistake in criticizing so strongly the fact that we are not trying to go too far at the beginning, but want to make our way with certainty as will be done under this bill.
Mr. MacNICOL; I want to make a few comments on the remarks made a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). I certainly do not like his attitude in the way of making a vigorous endeavour to belittle this bill. I have spoken to a great number of foremen and workmen in industry with whom I am acquainted, and he is not voicing the opinion of the ordinary workingman in reference to this measure. Their endorsation of all its clauses may not be one hundred per cent, but in general the average employee in industry-I cannot speak for those outside it, but I can say something for those inside it- endorses the present legislation.
Unemployment Insurance

The hon. member made some comparison of the number covered by the present bill with those covered by the act adopted in Great Britain in 1911. I do not think such a comparison is at all fair. The hon. member knows very well that the 1911 British act covered about 2,225,000 to 2250,000 out of 15,000,000 employees. The present Canadian bill covers 1,701,834 out of less than 3,500,000 employees. In that particular I maintain the present Canadian bill, which I quite agree might be amended as time goes on, compares very favourably with the first British act of 1911. My hon. friend therefore is entirely wrong if he intimates that the number covered by the present Canadian bill is not much greater in percentage than that covered by the first British act of 1911. The Canadian bill covers a little over fifty per cent of all those employed in this country to-day, whereas the British act of 1911 covered as I said a moment ago, about 2,225,000 out of 15,000,000 workers.
The hon. member also said something about a flat rate of contribution. A flat rate may have some merit or demerit, but so far as I can ascertain only two countries to-day have a sliding or percentage rate based on wages. Those countries are Germany and Poland, in which two countries the rate is made by a percentage of the wages. For instance, in Germany the employer pays three and a quarter per cent and the worker pays three and a quarter per cent on wages. In Poland the employer pays one and a half per cent and the employee pays one-half of one per cent. In other countries with contributory insurance schemes, for instance, Queensland, Austria, Bulgaria, Italy and Great Britain, the rate is a flat rate as is proposed in the bill for Canada. The rate is not the same in the countries I mention, but it is after the manner of the Canadian rate. Therefore the contributions proposed in the Canadian law conform to those of the nine states which have compulsory contributory unemployment insurance excepting Germany and Poland.
Just toward the close of my hon. friend's remarks, he said something about the present bill being comparable to a very tiny egg. The hon. gentleman is wrong in that. Workers in industry in making comparison of the scope of the Canadian bill with that of the bills of other countries find that the proposals made in our legislation compare very favourably with the best schemes in the other countries, and the two best are those in Great Britain and Germany. And further, to the British act, adopted in 1911, there have been

twenty-five or thirty major amendments since, as well as minor revisions, and I believe there is a bill before the British house now either adding to or amending the act. I feel that this present bill is a good start. It may not be all we want, it may not be all that is hoped for, but as time goes on we shall watch its operations. I shall do so very closely, and if in my contact with industry and managers and foremen and employees I see that it can be improved, I shall gladly support any necessary amendment in the future. But I feel that the hon. member who claims to represent labour should not take the vigorous attitude he does against this act. What the workingman wants to-day is to get the bill enacted, so that the 1,700,000 odd whom it embraces may sooner have an opportunity to participate in its benefits in the event of their being unfortunate enough to be laid off. I do not think the reply of the acting Prime Minister is quite right. He suggests that this is actuarially sound, that it is on the basis of a certain percentage being contributed by the employee, a certain percentage by 'the employer and a certain percentage by the state. But if the sum total of these three contributions is not sufficient to enable these people to live then it seems to me it is at this stage that we should ask whether or not that basis is correct. I do not see why the state should not contribute double or treble this amount if the scheme as actually worked out does not provide a sufficient living during periods of unemployment for those who are supposed to draw benefits. It is all very well to say it is on an actuarial basis and silence criticism in that way, but we have to get behind that and ask the basis of the actuarial computations. The basis is that the state, the dominion government, is giving very little indeed, and the greater part of the burden falls upon the worker and the employer. Undoubtedly the employer will pass his part on to the general public so that the state, as an organized body, is not contributing very much. The result very well may be that the people benefiting in this way will receive considerably less than the people actually on relief. It is going to be a serious state of affairs if the people benefiting under the unemployment insurance scheme will be in receipt of less than the people who have to depend entirely on charity. It is not going to commend the bill or even its extension to the favourable consideration of the public.

The point
raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is exactly the one we should take into consideration at this stage. My own impression of this bill is that it is going to have the general effect of reducing relief rates in cities where labour, highly organized, has succeeded in securing a fairly adequate measure of relief. Under this bill the total allowance, provided the full scale is drawn, will be $6 a week or $24 a month for a man. For his wife it will be S2.70 a week or $10.80 a month. He will receive ninety cents per week per child, and if he has three children that will amount to $10.80 a month. Then the total allowance under this scheme would work out at $45.60 a month; that is the total
benefit procurable by a family of five in which the father is the sole gainfully employed person. The present rate of relief to unemployed families of five in the city of Edmonton, where labour is well organized, is $53.75, with no contribution being made. After all what attraction is it going to have for the workers of this country if they find that they have been able to secure as much or more without making contributions as they will be able to secure under this scheme after contributing for two years?
