On further questions w'ith regard to the nature of these permanent buildings, I was informed that they were to form the nucleus of an arsenal, a place in which would be carried out the manufacture of ammunition, and that the present cartridge factory in the city of Quebec was to be removed to Valcartier. This cartridge factory at Quebec employs approximately sixty-two persons. During the year 1929-30, the payroll was $61,241.05, and during 1933-34 it was $41,038.29. I object to the work being carried on by the population of this camp, on many grounds, the first being that it is a distinct violation of the promises, pledges and even the actual program of the government, to employ hundreds of thousands of people throughout the country at a wage of twenty cents a day. We have been told that one of the principal pieces of legislation to be brought down during this session is a minimum wage measure. May I point out to the minister that it is not at all necessary to bring down a bill of this nature, or to ask the house to ratify a convention made in Geneva, in order to give reasonable wages to men employed in government concentration camps. These men are being paid twenty cents a day, and I believe they are being paid at this rate in violation of a statute of this parliament. I am under the impression that by a statute passed I think in 1930-and I shall perhaps be able to find it later-all employees on government work were to be paid at prevailing rates, which were specified at thirty cents an hour. By what authority and right the Department of National Defence is now paying those men twenty cents a day I have yet to be able to find out, unless it be that by authority of an order in council which permitted the creation of those camps a salary of twenty cents a day was authorized.

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
But if such were the case, the statute which applies to work on government construction and so forth should have been specifically modified or repealed for the purpose of carrying on this work. May I point out that by one stroke of the pen, by the passing of an order in council, reasonable wages could be restored to those men. The effect on the community would be to raise the general standard of wages throughout, and the effect on the men themselves would be to give them back some of their self-respect which they cannot possibly have if they are confined in camps such as these and paid the niggardly wage of twenty cents a day.
The second point I wish to make is that in connection with this particular camp the men are carrying on wrork which could be distributed and given to the tradesmen, artisans and workmen of the country. There is in the city of Quebec a very large number of carpenters, masons, men skilled in the construction trades, and we are deliberately setting these married men aside, allowing them to remain on relief, in order to give employment to persons in these camps. I pointed out at the time this legislation was introduced two or three years ago that there might be some justification for this when the works which were being carried on were not permanent or could not be carried out by persons in the community, but there was no justification for taking twenty cents a day men and giving them employment which would take away the bread and butter from the married men of the community. It was in reply to those remarks of mine that the Solicitor General, I think it was, stated that there was no danger of that. In this particular instance we are building an arsenal within fifteen miles of the city of Quebec where there is an ample supply of unionized labour, where persons who have been accustomed to carrying on construction trades would be only too glad to get work instead of remaining on relief. Yet this department is employing seventeen hundred men taken from all over the country and paying them twenty cents a day.
There is another point I might mention, although I do not want to touch on anything that might appear to be sectional. In other parts of the country where military buildings such as arsenals, drill halls, armouries are being constructed, these are being built under the Public Works Construction Act, and the men employed thereon are drawing reasonable rates of pay. Therefore I see no reason why within the district of Quebec we should not be allowed to enjoy the same

benefits as do people from other districts. It will be said I suppose that good work was done by men in these camps at the citadel at Quebec and Yalcartier, and I will not deny it. I suppose if it had not been for the concentration camp at Quebec citadel the ancient walls and fortifications would not have been repaired. But that does not alter the fact that the repairing of these walls would have given employment to a substantial number of men in Quebec who needed it, other than those now in the camps. I will not deny that there may be some justification for their employment in forestry work, I think in the United States they call work of that kind non-productive. As I understand it, in the United States the men taken care of in this way are employed in forestry operations and sometimes in the making of roads and trails through national parks. But this is an altogether different matter. This is a building the advisability of which is doubtful, being constructed by the aid of a special kind of labour which a great many people in Canada call slave labour; and at the very threshold of the place where that building is being put up are hundreds, aye thousands of married men on relief who are capable of doing this work.
In order to indicate the disapproval of at least of some members of the house of this particular form of government dealing with the unemployed, I propose to move:
That item number 17, national defence, salaries, be reduced by $1.
To one dollar?
By one dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough at the outset to say that he was directing his criticism rather against the policy laid down than against the present incumbent of the office of Minister of National Defence. I am grateful to him for that kindly allusion. On the other hand I do not wish in any sense to shelter myself behind that. He has stated it as his opinion that these single homeless unemployed men whose care the dominion government has taken over should not be paid a wage as low as twenty cents a day. I contend, and the government has contended all the way along, that this payment is certainly not a wage. How did the dominion government come into this position? They agreed with the provinces to take over the care of the single homeless unemployed, to clothe them, feed them, keep them warm, supply them with a small quantity of tobacco in the form of a ration, and give them such facilities for recreation as were possible. The only practicable way in which that could be

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
done was to collect them in camps in the various parts of the country. Some of those camps were taken over from the provincial governments, some were erected by this government. It was therefore necessary for the dominion government to come to a decision as to where the camps should be, and what work the men in them should undertake. It was considered, for I think sufficient reason, that this work at Yalcartier, laid out it is true for military purposes, could well be undertaken. In that camp the men were given food and clothing and the other things which I have mentioned, and over and above that provision which the dominion government on behalf of the provinces undertook with respect to the men they also supplied a small allowance of money, but certainly not a wage. The men had to do certain work, which was of a labouring kind. As the assistance of trained artisans was required, key men in the various branches of work were employed at current rates of pay. These key men were taken from the locality, and the key men received whatever wages men in that locality were receiving in these trades. The rank and file of the single homeless unemployed worked with the key men, in some cases under their direction, anyway in gangs which were led by them. The hon. member of course is entitled to his own opinion as to whether or not the policy laid down and carried out was a good one, but it is a policy which has been laid down by this government and it has in the opinion of the government worked out satisfactorily enough to be carried on as such.

The justification offered by the minister, that a certain number of men receive prevailing rates, seems to me only to make the matter worse. It would appear then that a few men-which I might tell the the minister were appointed by patronage at the request of political heelers of the constituency-obtained fairly good jobs. The remainder, who were doing just such work as is being done on building jobs throughout Canada, such as making cement forms and the ordinary work of the building trades, were receiving twenty cents a day. I understood the minister to say two or three nights ago that the cost to the government of maintaining these men in the camps was something like $1.30 per day. Am I right? That was exclusive of the overhead of the department, but included the cost of food, clothing and lodging. That plus twenty cents makes $1.50. It would have been a reasonable thing to add a further fifty or sixty or seventy cents a day and give employment to the people of the locality at not much more
expense to the country. It would have given a great deal of assistance to the persons most in need of government assistance at this time. I quite agree with the minister that something had to be done for the so-called homeless transient single men, but in order to do something for them it was not necessary to take the bread out of the mouths of the married men in the locality. That is the situation as it exists in the city of Quebec. This is not a non-productive undertaking; this is an arsenal, a building for the purpose of making ammunition. There is no reason why the district of Quebec should be treated differently from any other district. Here again I disclaim any intention of raising a sectional issue. It merely happens that I know what is going on at Valcartier; I do not know what is going on in the other unemployment camps. The men at Valcartier are doing exactly the same kind of work as men throughout Canada who are working on the public works program. That there was an agreement with the provinces to care for the homeless unemployed men, and that two or three or five or six out of each gang are being paid prevailing rates of wages, does not alter the fact that the government is having its construction work carried on at a miserably low rate of wages compared to that which a private individual would have to pay in the same part of the country. This is a bald statement of the facts. I contend that this government above all governments is not justified in reducing the standard of living by lowering rates of wages in order to carry out undertakings Which should be paid for the same as any other public works throughout the country.

Like the hon. member for Quebec South I want to say at the outset that any criticism I may have to make of the policy of the Department of National Defence does not apply in any way to the minister personally. I do contend, Mr. Chairman, that the minister must take full responsibility for the estimates of his department which he has brought before this committee. I notice that there has been a very substantial increase. At page 25 we find that in administration there is an increase of $41,000. In the non-permanent active militia there is an increase of $6,000, an increase of $54,666 for the permanent force and an increase of $15,470 for the Royal Military college, or a total increase this year of $117,136. I contend that if the minister cannot show good and sufficient reasons for the increase, these estimates should not pass this committee. I want to put one or two questions to the minister, and I hope that when I resume my seat he will at least endeavour

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
to give me an answer. First of all I want to ask what salary the chief of staff now receives, whether he was given an increase within t'he last two years and, if so, to what extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am perfectly ready to answer the hon. gentleman's questions, but may I suggest that they should come under the appropriate item. At the moment we are discussing civil government, in which there is a decrease, while the question put by my hon. friend comes under administration. Does he desire to proceed now?
With your permission, Mr. Chairman, and that of the committee I would rather proceed under this item. I do not see what difference it makes; the matter must come up for discussion anyway.
Mr. Chairman, in connection with the relief camps-
Just a moment.
Inasmuch as this matter does not come under this item I rule that it should be considered when the proper item comes up for consideration.
I would point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that relief camps are not mentioned at all under this item, which provides for salaries and contingencies.

The reply to the hon. member for South Perth, in that case, is simply that the minister had this point raised when he went into the estimates. One hon. member on this side asked if it would be all right to discuss these camps under this item, and the minister acquiesced.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am in the hands of the committee. I think hon. members proceeded to discuss relief camps under the first item because that matter might be discussed on several of these items. Certainly they come under civil government to a small extent, but the matter raised by the hon. member for South Perth is in no sense covered by civil government. However, if it is the wish of the committee to discuss everything under administration or civil government I have no objection. Administration will be the next item called.

May I suggest to the minister that it is somewhat difficult to know just where to discuss these matters. As I understand it the Department of National Defence are carrying on work which is paid for out of the general vote, which does not appear in the estimates at

all. I am rather anxious to know when we may discuss those unemployment relief camps. The difficulty under which we are labouring is that some of this work is being done by the Department of Public Works, some by the Department of National Defence and some by the Department of the Interior. We do want to discuss this relief item and this general vote, this lump sum which the government take annually, and we scarcely know where to find the proper item under which to discuss it intelligently. If the minister will give us an idea of just how he operates in his department with the relief sums that are voted to him, then we can discuss the matter much more intelligently under the proper items as they come up.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have not suggested any objection to a discussion of the unemployment camps under civil government, but the hon. member for South Perth asked a question with regard to something that is quite definitely under another vote. That was why I raised the question whether it was desirable to discuss that matter under this item. The last time these estimates were before the committee the whole discussion on the matter of unemployment camps took place on this item of civil government, and I suggest that if the hon. gentleman desires to discuss that matter it might 'be taken up under this item as well as under any other. The particular matter the hon. member for South Perth brought up, however, happens to come under administration, and not under civil government..
I thank the minister for his courtesy in saying that he has no objection to this discussion going on under item 17, and I assume that I am justified in going ahead.
On relief camps.
I will come to the relief camps eventually but I want to talk about something else in addition.
Anything that comes under this particular vote.

I put this question to the minister a few moments ago; I asked if he would be good enough to tell me if the chief of staff had received any increase in salary within the last two years and, if so, what that increase amounted to. While the minister is looking that up I would also ask him if any other officers of the staff received

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
increases in pay and, if so, who the officers were and what were the amounts of the increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: With regard to the chief of the general staff, his salary was increased two years ago from 88,000 to $10,000, less ten per cent.
Was the increase made retroactive for some months, at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, it was -not retroactive. I am informed that no other officers have received increases in the last two years other than those which would follow ordinary promotions.

The minister informs
me that the chief of staff had his pay increased within the last two years from $8,000 to $10,000. It does appear to me that an increase of $2,000 in the salary of any official here in Ottawa cannot be justified under present conditions, and I think that increase never should have been made.
I want to say to the minister also, in all kindness, that I think perhaps the greatest close corporations we have in Ottawa is the staff down at the Woods building. I well remember, and other hon. members of this house will remember also, that when the salaries of civil servants, members of parliament and senators were reduced, the measure which was brought into this house did not include the staff officers in the Department of National Defence. Later on it did include those officers; I am coming to that, but why was that not done in the first place? I have an idea that it was not done in the first place because the staff over at the Woods building runs the Department of National Defence. That ten per cent deduction finally did apply to these officers, but it was only after the opposition in this house and public sentiment throughout the country demanded it. They should have been included in the first place; they never should have been omitted. I want to give a word of advice to the minister, and I hope he will take it in the kindly spirit in which I give it to him. He has come to this department as a new minister, and I want to say that he should keep his eye and a firm hand on his staff over in the Woods building.
There are some things for which the minister must assume responsibility. He was sworn in as a minister of the crown on the 17th day of November, 1934. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, it appears that the new deal was first put into force in the Department of National Defence. I have under my hand a document by
which I believe I can prove my statement. The minister must take the responsibility for it, because it is dated December 20. 1934, just one month and three days after he assumed the responsibilities connected with the Department of National Defence.
I believe I would do well to take up the time of the committee to place this letter on record. The letter is headed "Department of National Defence, Militia service," and is numbered "M.3-1-8-3." It is dated at Montreal, province of Quebec, December 20. 1934, and is as follows:
District Circular Letter 11, 1934.
Officers Commanding.
P.F., & N.P.A.M. Units, *

I presume, Mr. Chairman, that all the military districts in the Dominion of Canada received the same circular. The letter begins: Mess Dress Ties
1. N.D.H.Q. Circular Letter No. 21. 1934, is quoted hereunder, for your information:-
(a)	"In view of the many different patterns and sizes of mess dress ties which it is observed are now being worn by officers of the Canadian militia, I am directed to request that all officers may be advised as to the correct pattern and size of mess dress ties and that such steps as are possible may be taken to secure uniformity.
(b)	Paragraph 49, Dress Regulations for the Canadian militia, 1932, prescribes a black bow tie, and this paragraph is being amended by-
And this is where the new deal comes in-
-adding thereto the w'ord's 'with square ends.' Ties with pointed ends should not be worn

I hope all hon. members will listen carefully to this.
-and the edges of the bow should be straight and parallel.
(c)	Particular attention should be paid to the dimensions of the tie, which should be about two inches wide at the ends and the length of the tie. in inches, should be twice the size of the collar, namely an officer wearing a 1 ;>* collar should wear-
And this is very interesting-
-a tie approximately 31 inches long.
(Signed) B. W. Brown,
Lt.-Colonel,
A .A. & Q.M.G., M.D. No. 4." Copies to all officers.
I submit that apparently the minister was the first to issue some of the new orders-the new reform-and this is very interesting. Perhaps the orders should have gone a little farther and the circular should have included something about the size of the hats the officers wear, recommending that the sizes be in accordance with the sizer of their heads.

Statesmanship.
Supply-Defence-Relief Camps

I ask the minister in all seriousness: under conditions now existing in Canada does he take the responsibility for sending that trash out to the officers of the militia? The thing is absurd. It is ridiculous, and is on a par with what I said a few moment ago-
Hear, hear.

-that the staff
officers-
A year ago.

I did not say it a year ago, but probably I shall repeat it another year. The staff officers of the Department of National Defence control the minister, the minister does not control them. I hope none of the officers of the Canadian militia will get into very serious trouble if they do not wear the right kind of tie or the right size of collar, and in carrying out the regulations of this overworked staff.
I should like to say one or two words more, Mr. Chairman. I am sorry I have not before me to-night a list of the militia buildings which have been built under the joint supervision of the departments of national defence and public works. Although I have not that list before me I believe it would make very interesting reading for the people of Canada. Since 1930 millions and millions of dollars have been expended in this way; some of the buildings are under construction, in an unfinished state, and some have been completed. These are military buildings. I want to tell the Minister of National Defence that he cannot make a military country out of the Dominion of Canada, and the sooner the government realizes that fact the better it will be for them and the country at large.
Under the items I have before me it would appear that the vote for the permanent force is increased by $54,666 over the amount voted last year. May I say a word about the permanent force. I have not much criticism to make about the rank and file of that force, but I do want to say that with a very few exceptions the officers are what I would call war lords, men who are attempting to create the feeling throughout the country that Canada must be prepared for another war.
Bunk.
Hon. members opposite are entitled to their opinion, and I am entitled to mine. But the fact that the new Minister of Trade and Commerce says "bunk" makes no impression upon me.

Oh, no.
fMr. Robinson.]

This country came
through one war. With the exception of some officers and a few non-commissioned officers of the permanent force, who gave good service, this country sent a civilian army overseas. I am willing to admit that, but I wish to say that had it not been for the young Canadian boys who enlisted and were trained overseas the Canadian forces would not have met with the success with which they did meet. However, I do not intend to dwell upon the war further than to say that if in the next fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five, forty or fifty years Canada should be unfortunate enough to be drawn into another war, we will have enough Canadians, men who were very young at the time of the last war, who could very well officer any army of the future. The expenditure of $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 a year to keep up a permanent force, most of whom are brass hats and men who send out circulars such as the one I have read, is a waste of money. Even if conditions were normal it would be a waste of money, but the waste is greater having in view the distress and unemployment common throughout the country.
Many buildings are being erected throughout the country. About $2,000,000 is being spent for an armoury in the city of Calgary, and in other places throughout the country. We had enough armouries in Canada during the war. Perhaps it was fortunate we had the armouries which were built prior to the war by the late Sir Sam Hughes. They were very useful. I will go so far as to say that the armouries which were built came in very handy. But we do not want the country studded with militarism and covered with armouries from coast to coast. If certain gentlemen in the employ of the government receiving $8,000 or $10,000 a year could possibly put over the propaganda, militarism would increase, but I do not think they will be able to do it.
In my opinion there is a great deal of waste in the money spent by the Department of National Defence. I-will not say anything about the relief camps, because other hon. members may take up that matter. I do say in all seriousness to the minister, however, that so far as possible he should cut out a lot of the red tape down in his department. The people of Canada do not want it; they expect something else. The minister, I think, has a wonderful opportunity if he will assert himself with the officers and the officials of his department, and instead of the officers running the department and running the minister, the minister should

Supply

Defence-Relief Camps
take a firm stand and control those who are under him, and if he cannot control them he should get rid of them. I go further. I say that the staff in the Woods building is overmanned. You cannot get into the place; they are like an army of chocolate soldiers down there. You can hardly get into the door. We do not want that in this country. I am fair enough to say that you must have a certain amount of discipline in a department such as the minister presides over, but there is a danger that you are going too far, and I think perhaps you have got to that point now. This country does not want to be ruled by war lords. I hope the time will never come when this country will be embroiled in another European war. It is all right to have a force for defence, and I am not offering much criticism of the active militia, although I think that a good deal of the money spent on the maintenance of the active militia is wasted and no good results come from much of that expenditure. 1 do repeat, however, that the money spent on the permanent force could be largely cut out and the service would be better off if many reductions were made not only in staff but in expenses.

Before this question was raised on Monday evening I had made an arrangement with the minister to take up the matter, so far as I was concerned, with the head of the department, General McNaughton. I had no particular desire to raise the question in the house, but the question was raised and I gave the house at least a part of what I would have submitted to General McNaughton. However, since Monday evening I have received further information to the effect that conditions in the camps in British Columbia are just' as bad as ever and possibly worse. I have before me an item that appeared in one of the Vancouver papers of February 28. I will read this item:
Relief Camp Deserters Prefer Gaol to Hunger
Twenty-eight relief camp deserters who some days ago were given the option of leaving town or serving three months in gaol after being convicted of obtaining meals by fraud in city cafes, gave themselves up at police headquarters Wednesday night. They expressed their willingness to serve their sentences as they had been without food for twenty-four hours.
The minister says that if a man has a grievance he may take it to the foreman of the camp, and if he does not get satisfaction from the foreman he can take it to the superintendent, and if he does not get satisfaction from the superintendent he can take it to the officer of the district. That may be true so far as the minister is concerned, but it is not
true in actual practice. A number of men in the camps have told me that the moment they bring a complaint to the foreman they are branded as agitators and told that if anything more is heard from them they will have to leave the camp. They are dismissed not only on the word of the foreman but on the word of the straw boss on the job. I have before me a note from a young fellow in a camp in Ontario. He complained about the food in the camp anid the foreman told him that he was an agitator, and that if he did not like the hash he could get out. But not only did he say that-and the same condition prevails in British Columbia; he also said, "I will see that you do not get any relief in Toronto." When they are sent out of the camp the provincial government and the city of Vancouver are advised to give them no relief, so that they have no alternative but to commit crime in order to obtain food. I was talking to one man who had been in four or five camps under a different name in each camp because he was blacklisted for "agitating" and dismissed from the camps. Now something must be done about a situation like this. The minister says that the provincial government can send inspectors into the camp at any time and inspect it for themselves, but the provincial government dare not send inspectors in because if the inspectors found fault with the camps it is just as likely that the federal government would say, "All right, look after the single unemployed yourselves." That is one of the reasons why the provincial government, even if it were anxious to see that the men are well looked after, will not take any active steps towards inspecting the camps. When we take the matter up with the provincial government they say that it is entirely in the hands of the federal government and that they have no jurisdiction; and when we take it up with the federal government, they in turn say that they are merely aiding the provincial government and not substituting for it because it is a provincial matter. Wherever you turn you are met with refusal to do anything. I think that the first essential in order to get some contentment in these camps is to see that the men in charge, the foremen and other officers, are men who have some of the milk of human kindness in their make-up. The minister says that conditions prevailing in the camps he visited were favourable compared with camps he had worked in. But these men are not in the same position as men working in construction camps. In the first place, they are getting the magnificent wage of twenty cents a day, and that is enough in itself to cause discontent. They have a
COMM ON b
Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
different psychology from men in ordinary work, and consequently the man who is competent to run an ordinary construction camp is not necessarily competent to run one of these camps; it needs an entirely different type of person. I suggest that if the officials of the department would give a little more consideration to the men in the camps and less time to considering the length of the ties worn at mess, things would go much better than they are going at present. I am convinced that we shall never have contentment in the camps-certainly we shall never have satisfaction to any great extent -unless the minister appoints men who understand the peculiar psychology that exists in these camps, or has an investigation made by an impartial tribunal who will fearlessly report on what they find.

After listening to the minister with a great deal of interest I want to say a few words in reply to. the statement he has made. When the hon. gentleman was appointed Minister of National Defence it ran through my mind, " Now we have a practical man who will surely see the necessity of a change of administration in the relief camps, especialy in British Columbia." I am very much disappointed and discouraged to-night to hear him say that in his opinion they are fairly satisfactory. I have a great deal of regard for the hon. gentleman and I must take his word for it that in his opinion the camps are satisfactory, but I do not think he has investigated the matter as carefully as he might have done. I have looked into it carefully myself. I know a good many of these boys, who have worked for me in the logging camps, and as the hon. member for Vancouver South says, conditions in these camps are altogether different from those that prevail in logging and construction camps. In the logging camps and construction camps the men get paid; they are there to make money and the contractors take care of the men, because otherwise they would not stay with them. But here the men are bound to stay. Now I suggest that the same condition could be brought about in these camps and there would be results; there would be something to show for the money that had been spent. For instance, if you put these men on for five hours a day at forty cents an hour, that would be S2 a day and you could charge them for their board. In other words, it would cost you $12 a week. Under the present administration it costs $9.10 and you get nothing done. They are supposed to be working but they are simply pussyfooting, and I do not blame them. But with an

additional $3 a week the men would work, everyone would be satisfied, there would be no more trouble, and at the end of the season there would be something to show for the season's work. As it is, you have nothing to show. I agree one hundred per cent with the hon. member for South Perth; the statements he has made are absolutely correct. Not only the Department of National Defence, but I think all the departments of the federal as well as of the provincial governments are overmanned. That is one of the factors that are holding us back. This is going to be tough for some of the people, but if I had my way, a number of highly paid civil servants would be looking for jobs. I am not picking on any particular men; if a man is required, that is all right, but a number of them not only in the Department of National Defence but in other departments are not needed.
I have nothing more to say than that there is too big a spread between $10,000 a year and twenty cents a day; that is the spread between the remuneration of men in the employ of the Department of National Defence. As I said before, I am very much disappointed in the minister. I have a high regard for the hon. member for Yale, who, being a practical man, knows what construction work is, but I think he will agree with me when I say that it is quite a different matter when you have a construction camp for logging or building a railway. In that case you have to take care of the men and pay them, and you will get the work done. In this case the situation is different; you simply have the men there, and in my opinion the way in which these camps have been and are at present being conducted is a disgrace tc the Dominion of Canada.

I should like to say a few words on this subject which seems to have appealed very much to hon. members from British Columbia. First, I think some of the statements made by hon. gentleman opposite in regard to conditions in the camps have been exaggerated. In the particular riding which I have the honour to represent, there are from twelve to fourteen camps; I have made a point of visiting them from time to time, and I would say that from seventy-five to ninety per cent of the men there appreciate the service that is being rendered by the department. There is of course an element which one could not satisfy under any conditions. I was present at one of the camps when a young man of about twenty-five years of age came up to the foreman and said that he was leaving; that he was going to take the train out for the east.

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
The foreman, who was a very fine type of man, talked to him like a father, but the boy turned and said: "I am twenty-five years of age; I have never worked a day in my life; I don't intend to either and I am taking the train." So he checked out. There is, as I say, in those camps a certain percentage of men who do not want work and who do not appreciate whatever might be done by any department of government.
Something has been said about the foremen. I think the foremen in every camp I visited and the superintendent of that division are men of the finest type. They are sympathetic; they give fatherly advice to the men and I think the men appreciate it.
The question of purchasing supplies was I believe dealt with the other day when this subject was up, and the department was criticized for not purchasing certain lines of products from local people. I have gone into this matter very fully, because I live in a district which produces great quantities of the products required by the camps. The problem which we ran up against was that of continuity of supply. It is impossible to expect any official to go around from farm to farm collecting a few sacks of potatoes here and there. When you have thousands of men it is necessary that you have a continuous supply from day to day. When dinner time comes along you must have the meat and the potatoes; you must have food for the men or you will have a riot on your hands. In different parts of the district the experiment was tried of having men collect from the farmers vegetables. and so forth, and in some cases meat. The supply was satisfactory for a very short time, but as I said before, it was found that it was impossible to maintain the supply. Let me repeat that I have found seventy-five to ninety per cent of the men in the camps appreciate the services rendered, and so far as the meals and accommodation are concerned I do not think there is any ground for complaint, because I believe the men in those camps are to-day getting perhaps better food than seventy-five per cent of the people in that district.
I have some criticism to offer, and I agree to a certain extent with some of the arguments advaced by hon. gentlemen opposite. I have been told by the department that this system is not permanent. I fully realize and I believe the department realizes, that a change should take place in the matter of wages. We have in British Columbia already what is known as the relief wage on works, twenty-five cents an hour. If the men were paid at the rate of $2 a day and were required to pay for their board,
clothing and other necessaries, they might not be as well off, but they would be a great deal happier and would feel better than they do to-day. After going into the question with some of the officials, I believe board of even a better variety than is at present being furnished could be supplied, including all kitchen expenses, at a rate of sixty cents a day. The men could pay sixty cents a day for their board and purchase their clothing from the camp as long as the stock lasted, say at cost, or anywhere they saw fit. If this were done it would be of benefit not only to the men themselves but to the communities in which their camps are located. It would create a sort of pay-roll for purchasing supplies from the local merchants, and I am sure it would distribute throughout the country a certain amount of money that is not being distributed at the present time.
In this connection I have pointed out to the department before, and it was brought to my mind the other day when we were discussing -the tourist business, that in the particular district which I have the honour to represent we have a large portion of what is known as the Cariboo trail, which I think I can state without fear of contradiction is perhaps the most scenic piece of road on the American continent. It lacks one thing, and that is the surfacing of the highway. If that highway were surfaced for one hundred and fifty to one hundred and eighty miles, it would bring to this country thousands of tourists and hundreds of thousands of dollars of revenue. But with the surface of the road in its present condition tourists would not undertake to make more than one trip on it, and when they returned home they would tell the people about the condition of that road. My proposal to the department has been- and I repeat it to-day-that we must cooperate in this work. There are camps located all about this highway, and if the thousands of men employed in the camps were paid a proper wage and the provincial government were to furnish equipment and materials, the work could be done. We would thus accomplish two things: we would put the men in a better position than they are in to-day; they would feel like free men, and we would be producing something that would bring a revenue to the country. This work -must be done in cooperation with the provincial government. I would advocate that the provincial government furnish all equipment and materials and the federal government the labour. They do not receive a direct benefit from the work performed; but it is only fair that when they have the care of these men and

spend large sums of money on 'the camps, they should do something along this line. The cost would not, as someone suggests, be doubled; it would mean an increased cost, but there would be a return from the expenditure made, not directly to the federal government but certainly to the province in the useful work that would be carried on in the way of improving that highway. Work of this kind could be done not only in that district but in others in which similar camps are located. I should like to leave that suggestion with the department. They have admitted, and we hope it will prove to be true, that this system of camps is not permanent; I believe under the conditions which are improving each day they will not last very long. But in the meantime I should like to see serious consideration given by the minister and his department to the proposal to place these men at a fair wage. I would not call twenty-five cents an hour a fair wage; it has already been adopted in our province as a relief wage. Even if we went a little further and made it forty cents an hour or two dollars for a five hour day I think would be fair. Having discussed this matter with some of the officials and the men I am sure they would be much more satisfied. This might not take care of one hundred per cent of the men, because there are men in those camps who perhaps are not physically fit to carry on this heavy work, and there are some who perhaps could not be made to work unless put somewhere where they can be controlled. But the large percentage of the men will appreciate this, and I think as far as their morale is concerned it is the only way it can be restored. I appeal to the minister and the department to consider this matter seriously.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence

Mr. Chairman, I well recall that last year when this matter was being discussed the Prime Minister explained that the barracks in Calgary to which the hon. member is referring was the barracks of the non-permanent active militia, which for the time being was used by the permanent force of military district No. 13 pending the time when provision could be made for a barracks for that district. This is that barracks, and it is for the permanent force, not for the police. This will enable the nonpermanent active militia to resume full use of their own armouries.
iMr. STEWART (Edmonton): I am sorry that I was misled by the explanation given by the Prime Minister last year; no doubt that was my fault. I fail to understand why a city like Calgary requires another armoury, as we call it, or barracks, when I do not know of another city in western Canada with a building of this sort. The impression I received last year was that probably the headquarters would be moved from Edmonton to Calgary. I well remember that I was confirmed in that impression because the city of Edmonton made a very considerable row over the matter shortly after the discussion arose in the house. I also recall that when this matter was being discussed the Prime Minister intimated that possibly there would not be a definite decision made with regard to the construction of this building, that the money might be used for some other purpose in order to provide relief. I think if my hon. friend looks up Hansard he will find the statement was made by the Prime Minister that nothing was definite about this. I admit at once that it was made after a good deal of discussion over this very matter, but do I understand that the city of Calgary is to have two fine, large armouries? The building located there now is a splendid armoury, of the regulation size, I should judge. Is this new building to house the Strathcona Horse? Of course that force has a splendid reputation and record, but why should it be continued and why should we

Supply-Defence-Buildings
continue to encourage and 'build up these forces in times like these and in a country like Canada? That is beyond my comprehension.
If it is definitely decided to go on with all this work, and if this is to be an additional armoury for the city of Calgary, all I can say to the minister is that I think the money might have been expended much more advantageously. One thing is certain, that this will not be relief in any sense, as we understand it in connection with the relief camps; this work will be paid for. I presume the cost comes out of the money voted under the general bill last year, but of course the Department of National Defence is in charge of the work. I do not know that I can make any further protest, but I will say to the minister that he had better pay very careful and close attention to the progress of this construction, which has been divided up in this way and the contracts for which have been let in this manner. Apparently the contractors have been selected and given the various units that are being constructed, with little or no competition except from others who were invited to be competitors. One can come to no other conclusion, and anyone who has had anything to do with public construction knows pretty well that it is not a very difficult matter for these gentlemen to get together and fix the price a building is going to cost. I want to register my protest against this sort of thing. If that is the method by which work is being carried on, either under the public works expenditure or with relief money, then I think the opposition are warranted in registering the strongest possible protest against this sort of thing. If one is to avoid criticism in letting contracts for buildings I would say the safest method to pursue would be that of allowing the general contractors to come in and do their bidding, rather than arousing suspicion by a selection of individuals who may tender on public works.

It seems we have mixed up expenditures on public buildings-mostly armouries-with a discussion on relief camps. I should like to say one or two things about each. It does seem to me that-I suppose we must say the government, but it has been true of other governments in the past-the government lacks imagination when it comes to expending public funds to provide work. I wish to protest as strongly as I can against the expenditure of vast sums of money on military buildings, arsenals, armouries or whatever they may be. In thinking over the things that Canada needs I would put additional armouries or military buildings at the bottom of the list rather than at the top. I can think of just a dozen other things which could be done. I dare say there would be constitutional objections, but one begins to notice that when governments want to get around constitutional objections they do not seem to have much difficulty. For instance, we could eliminate all level crossings in Canada. Of course that would be preventing people from being killed instead of getting ready for the killing of some more. We could carry out a large program of reforestation, something which is very much needed; and we could eliminate slums and build improved roads where they do not exist.

Supply-Defence -.Buildings

We could have sanitary equipment installed in homes already built, and could have extension of electrical energy to all houses in Canada. We could do all that. Then if we ran out of jobs we could have vast beautification projects, and could remove much of the man-made ugliness we find in Canada. One does see some very ugly things the removal of which would provide work. While the hon. member for Fraser Valley was speaking these ideas occurred to me. Oh, yes, we could have more post offices. Of course I do not know that we need clocks in the towers of all post offices, but let us have the post office buildings anyway. Then, we could have community halls through grants made by the federal government. Surely we do not have to go on with this stupid business of erecting more military buildings, especially in times like these, in order to provide work.
Now I come to the second point, namely relief camps. I wish I could agree with the optimism of the hon. member for Fraser Valley who thinks we soon will not have unemployment. I noticed only a few days ago the social services gave the number of those on relief as 1,350,000. That being the fact it would not look as though we would be free of unemployment for some time. If the minister insists upon all the expenditures being for buildings, I would suggest that we might build permanent homes for the unemployed, the people on relief. At the rate we are going it would seem that such action will be necessary.
I believe there are two points which may be argued against the camps as they are now conducted, one is that they are almost bound to undermine the spirit of the men. The second is that it is going to help continue the greatest of all our evils, namely the lack of purchasing power. The men in tthe relief camps are out of the purchasing group; they are not in a position to buy the things which other people want to sell. I think it would be very much better to spend even larger sums of money in public works, and to pay the men wages-not twenty cents a day; if only we could get around to doing something sensible and not spending the money in the erection of military buildings.
When speaking about the work which could be done I omitted to mention the reclaiming of the drought area. That would take a great deal of money and many men would be employed. Why not do it? But I think we are soon coming to the time-and as I sit here year after year I wonder how soon-when we are going to short circuit some consuming

power from the central authority direct to the people. I shall name some of the ways in which we could relieve our present difficulties. We could give or-I shall use the word again- short circuit purchasing power, without putting it through production, direct to all the blind in Canada. I suggest that would be infinitely more sensible than building more armouries. We could have a superannuation scheme for all people in Canada who desire it. I am not dogmatic as to the age at which such a scheme should become operative; it might be sixty-five years or it might be sixty years, but I do suggest it should be at a sum upon which they could live comfortably. In that way we could increase purchasing power and absorb into productive industry many of the young men who are in labour camps. It would be better to spend two, three, four, even ten times as much money as we are spending, and thereby absorb these unemployed people into natural public works and natural jobs such as they would have had if we had not gone through these trying days. It would be better to do that than to spend less money and run the chance-and we certainly are running the chance-of having all these people in camps forever unemployable.
Some may ask: Where would we get the money? I suggest there are two ways. One is to tax very severely large pools of money, whether through income, inheritance or business profit pools, and the other would be to draw upon the national credit. A person may again ask:	What is national credit? It
simply means that the federal government would be doing the trick the bankers have learned to do so well-the making of money out of nothing. Coupled with that would come an increase in the price of farm commodities, through a depreciation of currency. I am better satisfied to make what I believe is a more constructive approach to the problem of relief camps than simply saying that the men running them are not preparing the right menus and so on. I am sure the men running them are doing the best- they can, and I believe the minister is doing his best. I do not believe the present Minister of National Defence is responsible for the nonsensical expenditures suggested for military buildings. I believe he is a gentleman, and if he were allowed to do the sensible thing I am sure he would be only too glad to do it. But we have gone along stupidly for so long that if we did begin to do things according to common sense standards the shock would be too great. I can understand why the minister does not get around to it.

What is the principle that governs, if there is a principle? speechtext: Each case is judged on its merits. That is true but it
does not answer the question. Can public tenders not be called and the advertising, regardless of who the contractor may be, stipulate that local labour must be employed?

Before the item passes, I should like to ask the minister whether he would be good enough to give to the committee a list of the relief camps by provinces, where they are located, and the number of men in each camp.

No, so long as it is
on Hansard. Will the minister put it on Hansard?

Perhaps I might return to
the question of the unemployment camps which I was discussing some time ago. Before doing so, I am reminded, on listening to the discussion and on hearing the details set forth by the minister, of a speech made some time ago by a United States senator, in the course of which he exclaimed that they were furnishing certified food for the Louisiana hogs and building palatial residences for the Mississippi mules, whereas the people of the city of New York were going without food and clothing and being allowed to starve to death. Here we are with one-half of the brains of the Department of National Defence being utilized in order to ascertain just how long and wide a black tie must be worn with a mess jacket, and the other half in designing stables in Calgary for the Strathcona Horse, while thousands of men throughout the country are being employed at twenty cents a day to take away work from married men, artisans and labourers who are entitled, if anybody is, to get a day's work from this government. It is a crying shame and a disgrace to our country and our civilization.
But before leaving this subject, I would like to get from the minister answers to two questions. The first is: How does he get away from the fair wage policy, so-called, of this government and of the government which preceded it? I am now quoting from
