the Labour Gazette. This is the act of May, 1930. the effect of which is stated in the Labour Gazette of March, 1932, to be:
This act applies both to contracts for the construction, remodelling, repairs or demolition of any work for the government of Canada, and to works carried out by day labour, and provides for the payment of "such wages as are generally accepted as current from time to time for competent workmen in the district in which the work is being performed for the character or class of work in which they are respectively engaged: provided that "wages shall in all cases be such as are fair and reasonable;" also that "the working hours of persons while so employed shall not exceed eight hours per day."
That is the law. I am not quite sure whether the statute provides for day labour, but it certainly provides for contracts, and I think it provides for day labour on all construction work by any department of government. That is the law of the land. Am I to understand from the minister that there has been a derogation from the law in connection with these unemployment camps, particularly when they are carrying on construction work? I pause to ask the minister for a reply to that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: As I pointed out before, we do mot have to meet the difficulty to which the hon. member refers, because the unfortunate men who are without work and in the camps which are at present under discussion do not get wages; they receive food, shelter and certain other provisions, and they are given not a wage but an allowance of twenty cents a day.
So I am to understand that the answer of the minister is that because it is called an allowance he is permitted to violate the law of this country-
Because they do not call it wages.

-simply because they do not call it wages? This is what is stated in the Labour Gazette:
This act applies both to contracts for the construction, remodelling, repairs or demolition of any work for the government of Canada, and to works carried out by day labour-
And provides for the payment of wages- the government is obliged to pay wages; it is not obliged to get free work. The obligation entered into by the Canadian people with any person who is employed by the government of Canada is that he shall get wages. The provision goes further; it says that those wrages shall 'be at the rate prevailing in the locality; it does not provide and it never was intended to provide that by calling this
an allowance or saying it is free labour with a gift of twenty cents at the end of the day, the government can violate laws and repudiate the most solemn engagements entered into with the workmen of this country. I am anxious to find out by what authority this is done. I hate to use a word for which I might be called1 to order, but if it is simply by the subterfuge of saying that those men are not working for wages, I say to the minister that he is not serious when he tells us that. Those men are as much entitled to be paid as any other category of men. Simply because' they happened when the minister picked them up to be in such a position that they could not bargain with him, is he to say: We are not going to give you any wages at all; we are going to treat you as slaves? If any individual, any ordinary employer of labour, tried to do that in any province where there is a minimum wage law, he would be put in gaol-
There would be a Stevens committee.

-or there would be a Stevens committee, as the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard suggests. A very large number of persons in the industries which were severely criticized in the Stevens committee were glad to take wages of ten, fifteen or twenty cents an hour. They had never had any wages at all before those factories were established in their communities. Will he allow these sweaters of labour to say: "We are not paying them wages; we are paying them allowances," and thus get away from their responsibility? I think we shall have to appeal to a higher authority than the ministers who are at present in the house. It seems to me that all these radio sermons will have been given in vain if the very ministers in the cabinet are to be able to say:	We are not paying wages; we are
paying allowances; we will give the men a package of cigarettes a day and let them work eight hours. If that is to be the effect of any minimum wage laws or social legislation that may be introduced in this country under the aegis of these great reformers, I regret it very much, but I think the Canadian people will soon know what to do with such reforms and the advocates of reform as we have them on the other side of the house.
Let me tell the minister what I suspect is the authority he has. I suspect the authority he has for paying these slave wages-

Allowances.
Supply-Defence-Buildings

-is the peace, order and good government legislation; the very legislation which was crammed down our throats and passed by closure on the plea that it was to relieve the hungry, poor and miserable of this country is being imposed and enforced in order to lower the standard of living in Canada to a degree hitherto unknown. That is what I believe is the effect of the peace, order and good government legislation and what will ever be the effect of setting up a dictatorship in this country.
I come now to another point. The minister said that the department were spending SI ,200,000 in Calgary to put up a military building, erecting a stable for the horses of the Strathcona Horse and a mess room for the officers. Last year they spent at Val-cartier camp in Quebec 1507.889.35 for, among other things, erecting a building in which to manufacture cartridges for the army in case we ever again go to war. Why should the building for the horses in Calgary be treated so far as labour is concerned on a different scale from the building for the purpose of making cartridges? I cannot see any distinction in principle. I will tell the minister this: neither he nor any other minister would dare go into Calgary and endeavour to justify the erection of a public building with twenty cents a day labour. But he is going .to try to do it in Quebec.
The workers in Calgary are organized.

Our workers are organized, perhaps, but may not be so vociferous as those of Calgary, and they have not the same support in this house as the workers of Calgary have. Would the minister say that the Seaforth Highlanders armoury in Vancouver is to be erected by twenty cents a day labour? No fear. They would not dare to bring twenty cents a day labour into the city of Vancouver and take the bread and butter away from the people engaged there in the construction trades. Will they do it in any of the cities of Ontario? Will they do it in Belleville, where they are putting up a new gun shed. No fear. Will they do it in Kingston? Will they do it in Gananoque, in London, in Perth? No. But Quebec being a sane, quiet, conservative province, it is easy to say to our workmen: We will treat you well; we will give you an allowance of twenty cents a day. You do not have to be treated like the workmen of other parts of Canada; be grateful to the people who give you the job. My hon. friend says they did not even do it in

Montreal, but perhaps he is not quite right, because in fact a large proportion of the men employed at Valcartier come from Montreal; they are not from the district of Quebec. The people from the district of Quebec who are in these camps are those employed in the citadel, and they are neither homeless nor indigent men; most of them are farmers' sons from the surrounding parishes, and it is these people you are using to take work away from the citizens of Quebec.
I think it is only fair that the minister should explain first how he gets away from the so-called fair wage policy, and second what argument was used by him or his colleagues or anyone in his department to bring about the decision that in one part of Canada they should carry on construction works at a fair and reasonable rate for labour and in another part should carry it on with slave labour. I think we are entitled to an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In regard to the first reference that the hon, member has made, I have nothing to add to what I have already said. We do not pay a wage; we supply food and clothing and certain other assistance, including twenty cents a day allowance. With regard to why work is done in this way in one part of Canada and that way in another part, the work was devised in accordance with the requirements of the different parts of Canada. If there is a considerable number of unemployed men in Quebec as he has said, and there was desirable work to be done in that neighbourhood, the work was so done. In Alberta there is other work available for the single homeless unemployed for whom the dominion government is responsible. So there is in British Columbia; so there is in other parts of the prairie provinces. The men are employed in accordance with the requirements of the district where they are found in considerable numbers.

I would like to ask the hon. member for Quebec South one question. I understand that these were unemployed men who were brought or came into this camp, among whom there may be a few skilled workers. How is he going to use these men for construction work? Sometimes even in the building line men require brains, as they do in legal service. That may seem funny to the house, but it is possible. The difference between the two is that the builders produce something, while the legal services do not produce much, but live off the people. So there must be some brilliant labourers and some brilliant artisans in these unemployment camps. Would the hon. member for Quebec

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
South tell me how he is going to pay one man S5 a day and another twenty cents a day in that camp and have them in agreement?

It will not require any of the brilliance which is sometimes associated with the parasitic trade to which I belong to answer the hon. gentleman. Perhaps my hon. friend misunderstood me. What is going on in these camps is that skilled and unskilled labourers are building an arsenal. I am not urging the government to build an arsenal; as the hon. member for Southeast Grey has said, that is the last thing that is desirable, and it shows a remarkable lack of imagination on the part of the ministers that in this great crisis they can only think of putting up military buildings. But they are spending money to put up an arsenal with the labour of unemployed men. My hon. friend, I know, will feel, as I do, that those men should not be asked to do work which should be done by tradesmen and labourers of the vicinity. I think he will agree with me, now that he understands the question. Apparently he does not yet understand it. I shall have to send to Valcartier for some of those highly skilled artisans that he talks about to explain it to him. But now that he sees what it is about I think he will agree with me. My whole complaint-and I have been complaining for half an hour or more, probably too long-is that we are using that class of labour to carry on public works which should have been done under the Public Works Construction Act; that work of that kind should have been given to the unemployed married men who are on relief in the city of Quebec and vicinity where the work is being done. That is what should have been done; that is the whole point of my argument.

I would remind the
hon. member for Quebec South that it takes an artisan or mechanic anywhere from four to six years to learn his trade. Now he is telling us that in these unemployment camps they are using men who just come in there for the purpose of putting up buildings.
Don't you use day labourers in your country?

That is not the question. I congratulate the government on their brilliance in finding mechanics in unemployment camps who can construct a building. I never heard of it before. If you engage a man to do a little work around your home, which I hope you will be able to do to help the situation, you will find that there is quite a difference between a skilled mechanic and an unskilled man.

I am sorry to say that
having given myself to the service of my country I have no home. But there are something like 1,700 men in Valcartier camp, and whether or not they are competent to do the work, the work is being done. They are actually taking one brick and putting it on another, and taking a bit of cement and putting it on; they have a saw mill and are sawing up boards and taking them to another place and hammering them together, and that kind of thing. I do not know whether or not that is construction, but to me it looks like construction. Not only that, but the minister-and he is a good minister, such a good minister that he was selected from all the members from British Columbia to represent that province in the cabinet-this good minister in reply to a question put by me some time ago said they were building an arsenal. He did not say they were building it with artisans from elsewhere; he said they were building it with labour from that camp. It may be incomprehensible to my hon. friend, but that is what he is doing. Now does the hon. gentleman understand?

I have not said
anything with regard to these camps, because the ground has been so well covered by some of my colleagues. I should like, however, to join with them in protesting against these camps being placed under the Department of National Defence. That should never have been done. If we had had a labour department worth anything at all such provision for the unemployed would have been put under the labour department, where it ought to be. It is almost adding insult to injury to place the unemployed under the control of the national defence department. I am not suggesting that much of the work has not been well done; I think it has. In many ways the men are better in these camps than they might be in the congested quarters in which some would be living in the cities; nevertheless it is not a policy that as a country we should adopt in dealing with the unemployed.
Then I should like to join with my friend the member for Southeast Grey in saying that the kind of work which men should be called upon to do is necessary work. I need not traverse the ground that she so admirably covered as to the many projects that are very much needed in this country, this only half developed country of ours; yet we go on making the men mark time, as it were, for they cannot throw themselves with any enthusiasm into most of the work

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
they are required to do in these camps. I also feel that we are under a considerable debt of gratitude to-night to the hon. member for Quebec South for having put the case of the men so strongly. Although we say we are offering them a living, men in this country should have much more than a living. In reality it is not a living, it is only a poor subsistence. I am not going to worry whether they get a sufficient number of ounces of food to maintain them; perhaps they do. But it is a serious indictment of the policy of this country when the hon. member for Fraser Valley says that these men are getting better food than the majority of the people. I think it is a terrific indictment if the majority of the people in Canada are getting worse than they are getting in these camps. But it is not so much the quality of the food or this or the other detail; it is that the people of this country have a right to a full life, and these men are not getting a full life. You say they go into the camps voluntarily. That may be true, but what are the alternatives? As a rule the alternatives are simply two, either crime or starvation; those are the practical alternatives. When these men go out and attempt to carry on in an irregular way they are run in as criminals, but the only other alternative is for them to starve. Under such circumstances they go into the camps voluntarily. I am not so much concerned with whether they are skilled or unskilled, but I think it a serious thing that we should permit men who have spent many years in acquiring a trade to work for twenty cents a day, as I have seen them work in these camps. It is almost as bad to have unskilled men who could make a decent living if they had an opportunity working for the same small amount, call it an allowance if you like.
I am not going further into that matter to-night. On behalf of my constituents and others in this country I want to protest against the enormous expenditures which are being made in Canada for military purposes. We have formally declared that we have abandoned war as an instrument of national policy, yet we are constantly spending large sums in war preparations. I quite freely grant that as compared with certain European countries, even with England, or as compared with Japan our military expenditures are not heavy-
How about Russia?

Or Russia; quite so. Their military expenditures are heavy. I quite agree that compared with these countries 
Canada does not spend a great deal, but I submit that in comparison with other expenditures in this country these sums are very heavy. If you put all the expenditures for national defence together, including the militia services, the naval service and aviation, most of which comes under this department, you have a total of about $15,000,000. Then if you take our mounted police, which is practically a military force, you have another $6,000,000. There you have over $20,000,000, and on top of that you have these expenditures being made for elaborate public buildings for military purposes. The case of Calgary has been cited already. We have the barracks for the militia; we are to have a new building for the permanent force and we are told that in addition we need some sort of home for the mounted police, all in our little city of Calgary, and the same is more or less true of some other cities. Where are we getting in this country? Some of us had imagined that Canada was a peaceful country, but this does not look very much like it. We cannot find the money for peace purposes. Why, it was only to-day at noon that I happened to be attending a meeting of the executive of the League of Nations Society, and I found them struggling to get enough money to carry on the distribution of their literature. They receive a net grant from this government of something like $2,000. The government can spend some $20,000,000 in national defence, but the same government throws out a mere $2,000 to an organization that is trying to support the policies of peace for which the League of Nations is supposed to stand. So we have $10,000 given to the national defence department and the allied services for every one dollar given to such an organization as the League of Nations Society. I am not here to point out the excellent work that is done by that society, but I think that is a fair way of looking at our expenditures. We spend enormous sums on national defence, so called, but we spend very little on those constructive measures which might prevent us from ever being dragged into another war.
We have a new minister this year, and I should like to direct to him some questions which I have asked his predecessors and to which I have received no satisfactory replies. Why the expenditure of this $15,000,000 by his department? For what particular purpose is this money being spent? When we consider the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, for example, we ask them why they are spending the money and they tell us of this, that and the other thing which they have in view. I should like to ask, and I think we

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
have a right to hear from the minister, why we need this huge expenditure of $15,000,000 in this peaceful country of ours. Has the Department of National Defence a policy for defending this country? If so I think the house should know what it is. I should like to know whether the minister has met with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who I suppose in this case is the Prime Minister, who perhaps is overloaded with other duties and has not much opportunity to devote himself to external affairs. Even at that I would ask if the Minister of National Defence has consulted with the Secretary of State for External Affairs as to the general policies of Canada with regard to foreign nations. One of the predecessors of the present minister told me across the floor of the house that the only reason we needed an army in Canada was to keep our own unruly elements in order. I can hardly believe that he was serious in that statement, but if he was we ought to know it. Does it take this $15,000,000 to keep the unruly elements in order? If it does I think a little larger allowance than twenty cents a day would go a long way in dissipating the unrest we have in Canada; I think it would go much further than $15,000,000 spent in repressive measures. But I do not believe that can possibly be the real reason why we have an army and a navy, such as it is, in Canada; I cannot think it is the real reason.
I take it that this is more or less of a hangover from the old days when, for some reason or ocher, we were under the impression that preparedness was an insurance against war. That was the old idea. Is the minister convinced that that is true to-day? Surely the last war must have convinced every thinking man that those nations which were the best prepared were among the greatest sufferers. Preparedness is no guarantee whatever that we will not be dragged into another war; the contrary is the ease. When we are armed we are more apt to be attacked, and sometimes perhaps we are a little more apt to exhibit an aggressiveness which is rather provocative to other nations. There would be no guarantee even if we had a large army that we would be saved from another war.
Now let us come to concrete matters. I think we ought to know who is the possible enemy that Canada is likely to face. I have said to previous ministers that I cannot very well conceive that we are going to fight the United States. I think we would be very foolish to attempt anything of the kind, and I do not think the United States has any hostile feeling towards her northern neighbour. Are we going to fight on the
Atlantic or the Pacific? I think we should consider these points. Then may I point out that if we are going to defend ourselves alone, this little army and this tiny navy that we have would be absolutely useless against any large nation. What could we do with our small army and navy, even with the air force, which seems to be growing? What could we do? The next question is, are we going to ally ourselves with some other nation? Are we going to throw ourselves into a defensive alliance with the United States? That has been suggested by some people. It has been said that if Japan, for example, should break loose across the Pacific and threaten the Pacific coast, then the only possible thing for us to do would be to join forces in some way with the United States. I do not know whether these two boats of ours that now convoy the seals from the United States border up to Alaska are supposed to be sufficient to guard our shores against the attack of Japan; I cannot think it. Then are we going to enter into some sort of defensive alliance with the United States? The Secretary of State for External Affairs has never informed us with regard to that matter. I hope that when his estimates come up some hon. members will raise the question. If someone else does not do it I think I shall 'be tempted to do it myself, because I think we should know. I mention it at this time because it does seem to me that the policy of the Department of National Defence ought to be very closely correlated with the policy of the Department of External Affairs.
Are we proposing to enter into an alliance with the United States? On the other hand are we proposing to back up Great Britain? There have been suggestions in the last few months that the presence here of certain high officials from Great Britain would lead us to believe that some arrangement was being developed under which we would have a sort of imperial defence alliance. I should like to ask the minister, before he is through with this item, to tell us whether there is any ground whatever for believing that he or any of his officials have entered into any arrangement with Great Britain with regard to national defence. Is our air force to become a unit in an imperial air force? In considering these matters I think we have a perfect right to know whether or not something of that kind is in the wind. Further than that I think the Canadian people would like to know what the position of Canada is going to be if a war should break out in Europe, which is not an impossibility. I

remember once mentioning this matter two or three years ago and one of the ministers answered by stating simply that when I referred to war I was encouraging war. To me that is the veriest nonsense. In my view we ought to be open eyed and open minded enough to look at the possibilities. If a war should break out in Europe is Canada to be called upon to go to the defence of the motherland or of some other nations in Europe? That is a question which should be answered. I believe I would be expressing the opinion of what could be called the ordinary man in the street were I to say that if a European war broke out no Canadian troops would be allowed to leave this country to go to Europe. I believe that would be the general feeling. I should like to knew whether or not that is the policy which has been adopted by the department, or whether they contemplated that Canada at some future time again might be called upon to go to the help of Great Britain in connection with some trouble concerning which until that time we had had nothing whatever to say.
Then there is the further matter of our relationship with the League of Nations. Any person who has followed closely the work of the League of Nations will know that again and again there have been discussions as to how far Canada would be involved in the event of a war breaking out in which league members were involved. I know that Canada has signed that part of the treaty with some reservations; yet we are part of the league. We would call upon the league to assist us if our borders were being attacked. Have we any responsibility towards other nations? Is it wise that our air force, we will say, should be internationalized so that it might act as a police force and go to the help of any nation finding itself in difficulty? We have never to my knowledge had a frank discussion of such matters in this chamber. Year after year we have come here and voted 810,000,000 or $20,000,000-enormous sums- but we have not inquired what all this money is for. I am not blaming the minister for not hitherto having made a statement on this matter, because he has only recently taken over the Department of National Defence. He is an intelligent man; surely he must have made some sort of survey of the whole situation. That is his department; that is his job. I say that we in this House of Commons are entitled to know something about the conclusions at which he has arrived, [ Mr. Wood s worth. ]
and that we should not simply go on voting these moneys for purposes which are very vague indeed.
I have no doubt some of the newspapers will report me as saying that, assisted by the hon. member for Southeast Grey, I made my annual protest against war. Yes, but these matters come up annually, and I am convinced the only way in which we can represent our constituencies and make our contribution to the general welfare is by stating frankly when these matters are brought before	the	house what	we	believe.I was present,	and	I believe a	good manyother members	were present, at	the	Capitoltheatre to see	the	showing of	the	picture
Lest We Forget. Unfortunately I was not in a position to attend until rather late, but I did see part of the picture. I do not believe anyone could see that picture without being stirred-stirred not because it showed that finally the allies were victorious, not because some of the heroes of the war appeared on the screen and were cheered, but stirred by the thought that in a great modem war the individual is absolutely helpless, that it is all such a waste of human life and heroism. It is all a waste. One is almost obsessed with the utter helplessness of all in it. You saw those poor German boys coming up, and you felt pity for them. "They ought never to have been called to the front," you say? Yes, but our guns were blowing them to smithereens, just as their guns were mowing down our Canadian boys.
We cannot do anything about it.

I think I hear
someone say, "We cannot do anything about it." That is just where I differ from my friend across the way. Surely we as intelligent people must not simply throw up our hands in despair. A year ago I had the opportunity for a few moments to speak to a group of returned men, and I ventured to say to them that I thought their job was not complete until they had established peace in the world. I believe that is true; their job is not complete, and our job as citizens is not by any means complete when we choose simply to sit down helplessly and do nothing while all the time war forces are steadily extending themselves.
I suppose I am as proud as anybody of Great Britain; I think I am, but I am not proud of the fact that so far as we can see Great Britain is simply falling in line with other nations and building more and more

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
ships, thereby adding more and more to her military equipment. I suppose Great Britain has as much right to do that as has France, Germany or other nations; but that is not the point. I hope no hon. member will say, Oh, well, this is being said simply because I am against Great Britain, or something of that kind. That is not the idea. I go back to the atmosphere of last night's picture, and I believe no one could easily get away from the idea that we must rise above narrow nationalism if we are to get anywhere in the solution of this great problem. That is my reaction. We must rise above narrow nationalism and that narrow nationalistic spirit which has characterized us in the past, if we are to find a solution of the great world problem which confronts us.
At this time, when the estimates for the Department of National Defence are before us, I take the opportunity to state that if we simply pass them and year after year say nothing, we are not doing as much as intelligent citizens of Canada should do towards the solution of the peace problem. I do not think we are. I object to that fatalistic idea that the problem is too big for us, that we cannot do anything about it, and that we must sit down and let things go. Of course we say that if some of these times things break loose we will have a few trained men who will be able to organize our forces, drill us and march our boys away to a still greater slaughter than we had last time. I do not think that is good enough. Surely we know enough about science to-day to realize that every effect has some very definite cause. We are learning that in the medical realm; we know that certain germs are responsible for disease. Our social engineers and medical men have worked to get rid of many of the diseases which have harmed us in the past. I woidd urge that we apply similar reasoning and a similar technique to the great social problem now before us. I do not think that wars come out of the thin air. I do not think that they come, as we sometimes say, using a pious phrase, by "act of God" in punishment for our sins. We know perfectly well that war comes from certain predisposing causes, and we in Canada, though a small country so far as population goes, are surely one country in the world which has very considerable influence. If we are fifth or eighth-whatever it is-among the trading nations of the world, and if we are allied with a great empire on the one hand and neighbour to a great nation, the United States, on the other, surely we are in a position to
do something to save ourselves from any such cataclysm as came upon the world back in 1914. I do not think we serve any useful purpose simply by going out and praying, "Give peace in our time, O Lord!" No, that will not bring peace. We have to do it in a more constructive way than that-a much more constructive and more definite way. So I plead while these estimates for the Department of National Defence are under consideration that the minister give us some outline as to what is in his mind, and as to what is in the minds of officials of the department with regard to the purpose for which these funds are being expended. Further than that, if I am not considered too idealistic, I should like to have this chamber devote a little bit of time before the estimates are passed to a consideration of the definite and constructive steps which we might take towards making our contribution to world peace.
Would the Minister of National Defence be good enough to place upon Hansard a list of the relief camps, by provinces, where they are located and the number of men in each?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I understand that tables should not be placed on Hansard unless they are read to the house. I had the information in front of me, and for the past half hour I have been ready to read it, but at the present time it would not look as though there would be time to place the information on Hansard. It could not be completed by eleven o'clock. I wonder if it would suit the purposes of the committee if the information were tabled.
By consent it may be done.

I wish to say a few words, because it is obvious the committee does not intend to allow the item to pass to-night. As an ordinary citizen I resent the idea that Canada should be painted as she has been painted to-night by hon. members from various sections on the opposite side of the house, in an effort to show that so far as the treatment of the unemployed is concerned we are in a class by ourselves. Listening to this discussion, as I have been listening since eight o'clock, one would come to the conclusion that Canada alone of all the countries in the world has been having some trouble in regard to unemployment. No mention has been made by any speaker on the other side, whether among the Liberals or in the little group in the comer-and they can become more excited than the Liberals

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
on a question of this kind-no hon. member, I say, has admitted that at any time in the last four years the world has been going through a very serious crisis. No hon. gentleman has suggested or admitted that Canada is merely participating in a world wide crisis. But I make this statement, that Canada has come through the crisis better than any other country in the world, and I make no exception to that statement. I do not except Great Britain or any other country. According to the figures given out by Great Britain and by the United States, the two countries with which we most frequently compare ourselves, Great Britain has more unemployment according to population than we have to-day. Her figure is 2,500,000 and her population is four times ours. In other words, on that basis, we should have about 600,000 unemployed, whereas we have been 450,000 and 500,000. And in the United States it is admitted by the government itself that they have 10,000,000 unemployed. Indeed it is claimed by Green of the Labour group over there that the number of unemployed in that country is between 11,000,000 and 12,000.000, which is twice as large as ours, per thousand of population. There have been 30,000.000 unemployed throughout the world, yet Canada has taken care of her unemployed better than any other country.
The hon. member for Quebec South is usually pretty fair, but he is playing good politics; I will not question that. But he attacked us in regard to the relief camps and he called them slave camps. I do not think that was worthy of him. His predecessor of the same race who went to the provincial house used to talk about slave camps and I thought we were rid of that word when he left us, because it is ridiculous. H it is slavery to take boys who are running around getting into mischief, who have nothing to do, who have nothing to engage either mind or hand, and to bring these boys into camps and feed, clothe and shelter them, and give them a little money to spend while they are working in these camps-if that is slavery, then I know of millions of people in various parts of the world who would love to indulge in slavery of that kind.

They gave the same
excuse when they took the negroes from Africa.

And as the Minister of
Finance says, they go voluntarily to the camps; they are not driven there. One of my hon. friends from one of the Vancouvers complained bitterly because one of these men

had been called an agitator and had been turned out of the camps. He went under an assumed name to five or six different camps and was kicked out of each one. He must have been a rotten agitator and I imagine he was well kicked out. But he asked to get back into the camps; he kept changing his name, begging his way back into the camps, and he must have liked them. I am not trying to introduce politics into this. But because I speak in a firm or fairly emphatic voice I am accused of playing politics, though my hon. friends can talk any way they like and that is not politics. I am merely stating the Canadian point of view when I say that I do not think it is good for this country that anyone should be continually describing conditions in Canada as if we treated our unemployed worse than other countries have treated theirs, when as a matter of fact we have treated ours better. No one can become so excited on this question as the hon. gentleman who has just sat down. One would think that he was the only man in this chamber who was interested in the Canadian people who are unemployed. I make this statement without fear of contradiction, that there is not a gentleman on the other side of the house or on this who is not just as much interested in the unemployed and in the poor as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-no one on either side of the house, either the lady member or any hon. gentleman.
Mr. Chairman-
Keep your seat; I have the floor.
I would ask that that expression be withdrawn. There is nothing I said that warranted such a statement.

I have nothing to withdraw. The hon. gentleman has stood up forty times in my hearing and in a loud and emphatic voice talked about the unemployed and the injustice done them. He works himself into a passion, and if he were full blooded he would burst a blood vessel; but he is not a bit more interested than anyone else in the unemployed except to appeal to the group who are unemployed, and appeal in a demagogic way. He is not a bit more interested in the unemployed than is any hon. gentleman either on the other side or over here.
And when he starts talking about peace, can he tell me one person in all this country who suggests anything but peace? Is there anyone in Canada who does not want peace?'

There are a few hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house who went over to the front, and I can say that there is no one in the whole world who wants peace more than the men who were at war. Yet the hon. gentleman talks about peace as if Canada were preparing for war. Well, after listening to a lot of this balderdash-
Mr. Chairman-
-I have copied down-
Mr. Chairman, I ask for your ruling as to whether that expression used by the minister-balderdash-is parliamentary or not.
It is the best I can think of.
I ask that the word be withdrawn.
It is at least better than the word humbug, which is so often used around this house.
I ask that the word be withdrawn.
I fancy that the minister did not apply that word to the hon. gentleman personally.
I do not understand the English language if he did not, and I ask that he withdraw it.
I do not withdraw it, because I apply it to what the hon. gentleman has said in many of his speeches. It is a description that can be given his speeches.
I rise to a point of order. I claim that the word is unparliamentary and the minister should withdraw it.
I submit it is not unparliamentary. It is as good a word as humbug or rubbish, and either one of those words would be applicable to a great deal of what the hon. gentleman has said.
I ask for your ruling, Mr. Chairman.
I must rule that the minister applied the word to the hon. gentleman's opinions.

I should like to put on record-

I am sure that all nations are trembling as to what we shall do with this great military power of ours.
We talk about the treatment of our people, and we hear a great deal about the wickedness of capitalism. Well, there is only one country that has tried anything but capitalism and that is Russia. And Russia has had in the last year at least 5,000,000 people who have starved to death.
And they have the biggest air force in the world.

Yes, and some of the greatest military defences of all kinds. No one realizes more than I do that there have been some

terrible errors committed by capitalism, but decent people of all parties in this country are trying to work out something in the way of a remedy for the condition that exists, and I submit that we should not take the attitude of always belittling our own country. We should not take the attitude that Canada has done so badly, because the fact of the matter is that she has done better than any other country in the world.
